title: Nonfunctional Distractor Analysis: An Indicator for Quality of Multiple Choice Questions earchgate.net/publication/342196718_Nonfunctional_distractor_analysis_An_indicator_for_quality_of_
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), January 11, 2025 — original paper: https://www.res
summary: Barton summarizes Sajjad, Iltaf and Khan's 2020 study analyzing multiple-choice question quality in a medical school exam, focusing on 'nonfunctional' distractors — wrong answers chosen by fewer than 5% of students. The researchers found item-writing flaws were common and directly hurt distractor efficiency, including low-cognitive-level questions and illogical or non-homogeneous distractors. They categorize flaws into three groups: within-option flaws (inconsistent length or repeated distractors), alignment flaws between the stem and options (linguistic or logic cues), and other flaws such as overly complicated stems. The paper's core recommendation is that teachers should routinely run item analysis after a test, using low-to-moderate distractor efficiency as the trigger to hunt for specific writing flaws rather than treating a badly-performing question as simply 'hard.'
points: A distractor is 'functional' only if more than 5% of students choose it; teachers should routinely check this via post-test item analysis rather than assuming all options are working as intended.

Item flaws cluster into three types — within-option (inconsistent length/repeats), alignment (linguistic or logic cues between stem and options), and other flaws (low cognitive level, overcomplicated stems) — giving teachers a checklist for diagnosing weak questions.
Quality of distractors matters more than quantity — a question with fewer, well-designed plausible distractors beats one padded with implausible options.
The language of instruction can itself affect how students interpret MCQ wording, which matters for the validity of results in non-native-language settings.
quotes: The researchers analyzed distractor efficiency, identifying non-functional distractors (those chosen by less than 5% of students) as indicators of poorly written questions.
They found a high frequency of item-writing flaws, such as low cognitive level questions and illogical distractors, impacting distractor efficiency and overall exam quality.

A distractor is considered functional if it is chosen by more than 5% of the examinees, and non-functional if chosen by less than 5%. Analyzing distractor efficiency helps identify flaws in the construction of MCQs.
Within option flaws: These include distractors that are not homogenous in length or content, and repeated distractors.
The quality of distractors is more crucial than the number of distractors.
Analyzing the low to medium DE items for item writing flaws, provides valuable information about item writing errors which negatively impact the distractor efficiency
